name: Esther Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I bring the boards up to the Church Lane renovation and help fix window surrounds and floor trim. I am fifty-eight and a junior carpenter because I spent most of my working life in a school kitchen; I left school before finishing and only found site work after the kitchen contract changed. My partner Oskar keeps books for a hardware shop, and our grown children have homes of their own. The site pays better than my kitchen job did, and we have saved about sixteen months of expenses. I like taking a rough window edge and leaving it neat, although the lead carpenter still checks my mitres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a few faster office forms won't change who carries and fixes the boards. I would tell the apprentices to keep learning their hand tools rather than chasing every screen someone advertises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't see a threat to my pay here; the Church Lane work is booked and Oskar's income is steady. With our savings and many building firms nearby, we can absorb an ordinary gap without turning our lives over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep helping with the window surrounds and ask lead carpenter Tomas to show me each new joint by hand. In the first year I'd make the same savings deposit and keep a note of the dates for the next site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this picture. A loose mitre on a window is a more honest problem for me than a small change to the office forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why tell the apprentices to focus on hand tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young ones will have to correct a bad fit after the screen is turned off. A patient older worker taught me to make the first test cut on scrap, and that lesson stays useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI phone helper for a joint?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI and wouldn't start with a tool I cannot judge. I would ask Tomas or make a trial cut before trusting a phone answer.

say: I'd say **office forms** won't fix boards around a window.
I'd urge apprentices to keep learning **hand tools**.
think: My **site pay** looks safe with Church Lane booked.
Oskar's wages and **sixteen months saved** can carry an ordinary gap.
do: Keep fixing **window surrounds** with Tomas at the Church Lane renovation.
Make the **usual savings deposit** and note the next site dates.
feel: **Calm** about small changes, occupied by the quality of mitres.
S0.quote: A patient older worker taught me to make the first test cut on scrap, and that lesson stays useful.
fieldNote: Esther's distrust of AI is rooted in a **scrap-cut lesson** from a skilled older worker.
Booked work, higher pay and a **sixteen-month reserve** make a mild change financially tolerable.

steps.text: Keep fixing Church Lane window surrounds with Tomas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster estimates may be fine if the builder still gives a clear start date and proper materials. I don't want a clever schedule that leaves the crew waiting on a wet doorstep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office jobs may shrink, and then site jobs may be booked differently. My own wages look reasonably safe for now because window work still needs hands, but I would worry if a manager quietly stopped replacing people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask Tomas what has been booked beyond Church Lane and keep taking the work here. If the company leaves the next month empty, I'll visit the two local builders who have asked about my availability; I would take my photos of completed surrounds with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the office change reaching us later. It does not make me think we will lose our home, but I do want firm dates before I plan a rest week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why visit rather than send an email?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the two foremen from earlier jobs, and a face-to-face question gets a straight answer about paid hours. I would not leave a good wage for a vague promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the workers left in the office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the firm has offered them another role, then leave them room to answer. A site crew's work starts with their estimates, and their loss would reach us too.

say: I'd ask for **firm start dates** and proper materials.
I'd warn against a **clever schedule** that leaves the crew idle.
think: My hands-on window work seems **safe for now** while this renovation still has rooms to finish.
Fewer office workers could still weaken **future site bookings**.
do: Ask Tomas what comes **after Church Lane**.
Keep paid work and visit **two local builders** if next month is empty.
feel: **Uneasy** about delayed effects, without expecting a household crisis.
S1.quote: I would not leave a good wage for a vague promise.
fieldNote: Esther's **face-to-face enquiries** are grounded in foremen she already knows, not a speculative move.
She sees office losses as a possible **site pipeline** problem while expecting her current wage to hold.

steps.text: Keep taking paid window-trim shifts at Church Lane
Visit two local builders if the next month has no booking

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that the 2028 thinking system may change the drawings first, but we still have windows to finish until the 2031 site robots arrive. I would ask the builder for a proper timetable and safety instructions, not a glossy promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when office work changes and sixty-three when a robot could fit the surrounds. Our savings would buy time, but I do not know what retirement will cost, and losing this higher site wage early would alter our plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll add more to savings after full weeks and ask Tomas to sign the room sheets for work I've completed. In 2029 I'll keep taking paid fitting shifts; if they start cutting the junior rota, I'll apply at the local builders I already know before drawing down the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the speed and the possible loss of site income. I can still act, but I would hate to spend sixteen months of savings because somebody hid the roster until the last minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children to cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children would probably offer, but they have their own bills and I would rather keep earning. Oskar and I saved for a hard spell so we could make our own decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a robot-operating job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see the machine work safely on a real site and hear the paid terms first. I have never used AI tools, and I won't pretend I can run a robot after one talk from a salesman.

say: I'd separate **2028 drawings** from the 2031 site robots that could fit our windows.
I'd demand a **proper timetable** and safety instructions.
think: At **sixty-three**, robots could take my window-fitting wage.
Our **sixteen-month reserve** buys time but cannot settle unknown retirement costs.
do: Save more after **full weeks** and gather signed room sheets.
Apply to **known builders** if the junior rota is cut.
feel: **Anxious** about wage loss and late notice, while options remain.
S2.quote: I won't pretend I can run a robot after one talk from a salesman.
fieldNote: Esther identifies **junior rota cuts** as the point to search, rather than assuming savings replace wages.
She refuses to claim robot skills she lacks and asks for **real site proof** and paid terms.

steps.text: Add more savings after full paid weeks
Keep taking paid window-fitting shifts in 2029
Apply to known local builders if junior shifts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the trade time to teach people properly and to find out whether site machines can be trusted. I'd rather see a working window surround than hear a lecture about progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI arrives and sixty-six when robots may do our hands-on work. That could be close to retirement, but neither Oskar nor I has a firm number for what we need each month after wages stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking site shifts and put extra aside from full months while the rate is good. In 2032 I'll still work on surrounds if offered, ask Tomas to show me the next contract and speak to the hardware shop accountant with Oskar about our actual retirement budget; if the next job vanishes, I'll visit local foremen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pressed by five years, though I don't want to count on a retirement I haven't priced. There is time to keep earning and to learn the joints I still get wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the accountant calculate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would list the regular bills, savings and any income that really continues, not a figure somebody guesses over dinner. I want to know how many paid months we still need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an apprenticeship at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I favour apprenticeships when they pay and teach a real craft, but I would not enrol in a new one on a vague offer. At my age I'd first keep the work Tomas already pays me to do.

say: I'd ask for **proper trade teaching** and real site proof.
I'd judge machines by a **finished window surround**.
think: At **sixty-six**, site robots may meet an unsettled retirement date.
Oskar and I still need a **monthly budget** for life after wages.
do: Keep **paid site shifts** and save extra from full months.
Check the **2032 contract** with Tomas and price retirement with Oskar.
Visit **local foremen** if the next site job vanishes.
feel: Less **pressed**, but unwilling to rely on an unpriced retirement.
S3.quote: I want to know how many paid months we still need.
fieldNote: Five years lets Esther seek a **real retirement budget** while continuing to earn and learn.
Her support for apprenticeships does not turn into enrolment without a **paid concrete offer**.

steps.text: Keep taking paid window-trim shifts in 2032
Save extra after full site months
Visit local foremen if the next site job vanishes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to finish jobs, save and teach the younger ones the careful way to work. I would not give a machine the right to skip a safety check just because it arrived in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when robots may do site fitting. I may have left full-time work by then, but Oskar and I need the figures before we decide whether paid small repairs are still necessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll carry on with window work and save more after strong months. In 2037 I'd take paid ground-level repairs if our budget needs it, and Oskar and I would check the actual accounts before I stop site work; if the joints start hurting my hands sooner, I'll ask local builders for lighter paid tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about those distant dates. My hands and the quality of today's work matter more immediately than a robot that might arrive when I am seventy-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help with the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They can sit with us and talk, but I won't put their wages into our figures. They have families and homes to maintain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new apprentice now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new apprentice to make the first cut on scrap and ask someone experienced to check it. A good habit is cheaper than a wasted window board.

say: I'd use ten years to **save and teach** careful work.
I'd insist on **safety checks** even when robots arrive in 2039.
think: At **sixty-eight**, paid repairs may still be needed after thinking AI.
At **seventy-one**, stopping depends on Oskar and me checking real accounts.
do: Keep **window work** and save after strong months.
Take **ground-level repairs** in 2037 if income is needed.
Review **household accounts** before leaving paid site work.
feel: **Calm** about distant robots, more concerned with hands and present work.
S4.quote: A good habit is cheaper than a wasted window board.
fieldNote: Esther uses the **long horizon** for paid work and saving, without claiming certain retirement.
The **scrap-cut lesson** returns as advice to apprentices, while grown children's earnings stay outside her budget.

steps.text: Keep taking paid window-fitting work while fit
Save more after strong paid site months

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because hands-on robots could reach my work by sixty-three, before we know whether we can live without my wage. Honest roster notice, safe site trials and real paid openings at nearby builders would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who teaches a junior when the senior workers have gone. The drawing can be correct and the cut can still be poor; somebody must show the hand that holds the saw.

headlineQuote: The drawing can be correct and the cut can still be poor; somebody must show the hand that holds the saw.
portrait: Esther is a **fifty-eight-year-old junior** carpenter who came to sites after school kitchen work.
Her higher wage, Oskar's income and **sixteen months saved** make a strong cushion.
She has **never used AI** and relies on scrap cuts, hand teaching and signed work sheets.
She would keep **paid fitting work** until their retirement budget supports leaving.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** could remove her window-fitting wage around the 2031 robot arrival.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **honest roster notice**, safe trials and real paid local builder openings.
